opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something we actually ran into in practice, and I think the reason is fairly fundamental.

When you train a language model with next-token prediction, the hidden representations are organized around semantics: what concept is this, how does it relate to that, what comes next logically. The loss is essentially asking the model to compress meaning. Diffusion is asking for something quite different. The denoising objective rewards the model for predicting pixel-level or latent-level details: textures, edges, high-frequency structure, exact color values. A huge share of the gradient signal in diffusion training goes into reconstructing low-level information that has very little to do with abstract semantics.

So if you put both objectives into the same backbone and share the parameters, they compete for representational capacity, and they pull the features in different directions. Language wants features that are abstract and invariant. Diffusion wants features that preserve fine detail. In the middle layers especially, you see the representation drift toward something that is good for reconstruction but less clean semantically. And the diffusion loss is often numerically large and noisy across timesteps, so if you don't balance it carefully, it dominates the optimization. The language ability degrades, sometimes in subtle ways: reasoning gets a bit worse, instruction following gets a bit worse, before you notice it on the obvious benchmarks.

There's also a deeper point I care about. People hope that generation and understanding will naturally help each other, that "if I can draw it, I understand it." But reconstruction-type objectives don't automatically give you semantic understanding. We learned this lesson already in vision self-supervised learning: pixel reconstruction gives you features that are good for some things but often weaker for high-level semantics unless you design it carefully. Diffusion inherits that property. So naively mixing it in doesn't add understanding; it can dilute it.

That's why I think the practical solutions tend to involve some decoupling: either separate the heavy pixel-generation part into its own module or decoder, let the language backbone work at a more semantic level, like generating high-level visual tokens or conditions, or carefully control which parameters receive diffusion gradients. The unified dream is attractive, but you have to respect that these objectives are not naturally aligned. Unification at the interface level is easy; unification at the representation level is where the real difficulty is.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that this isn't an intuition I started with. We ran into it. When we tried to put image generation and language into one model and train them jointly, the language side got worse, measurably, and we spent quite a while trying to understand why.

My current view is that it comes down to what the training objective actually asks the representation to do. Diffusion is fundamentally a reconstruction task. You add noise to an image, and the model has to recover the pixels, or the latents, as precisely as possible. That pushes the shared representation toward low-level, high-entropy detail: texture, lighting, exact spatial layout. It rewards being faithful to appearance.

Language modeling wants almost the opposite. Next-token prediction rewards compression. It wants the representation to throw away surface variation and keep the abstract structure: what the object is, how it relates to other things, what will plausibly come next. Semantics is, in a sense, what survives after you discard appearance.

So when you force the two to share parameters, they pull in different directions. The diffusion gradient says "keep every detail, don't abstract." The language gradient says "abstract, forget the details." And the generation loss tends to win, because reconstructing pixels produces a much denser, louder gradient signal than predicting one token. The representation drifts toward the visual side, and the language semantics get diluted.

There's a second, more subtle effect. In joint training, the text that pairs with images is usually captions. Captions are a very impoverished form of language. They describe what is visible, they're short, they rarely involve reasoning or long dependencies. If a large fraction of your text gradient now comes from caption-like data, you're effectively fine-tuning the language model on a degenerate distribution of language. Even without the diffusion loss, that alone would hurt.

So the way I now think about it is that understanding and generation are not symmetric tasks, and they shouldn't be treated as symmetric. The lesson we took was to protect the language backbone, let it provide the semantic conditioning, and give the generation component its own capacity rather than asking one set of weights to serve two masters. Otherwise you don't get a model that does both. You get a model that does both slightly badly, and the language side pays the larger price.

astra-6.text:
I think the key issue is that the two tasks ask the model to preserve different kinds of information. For language, you want representations that capture meaning—who did what to whom, how concepts relate, and what follows from a statement. For image generation, the diffusion objective asks the model to predict and remove noise, which requires a lot of information about visual appearance and spatial detail.

If those objectives update the same parameters, their gradients can interfere. The model may start reorganizing its representations around what helps reconstruct an image, even when that is not what helps it understand language. And if the image objective contributes disproportionately to training, that pressure can become stronger.

So I wouldn’t say joint training necessarily damages language semantics. The risk comes from how you share parameters and balance the objectives. Ideally, the tasks share useful conceptual knowledge while keeping enough specialized capacity that learning visual detail doesn’t overwrite the structure needed for language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key issue is that the two objectives ask the model to learn different things. Language modeling pushes it to capture meaning and relationships between concepts. Image diffusion pushes it to predict and remove noise from a visual representation. That requires a lot of attention to local details—texture, color, spatial structure—which don’t necessarily help language understanding.

If those tasks share parameters, their gradients can interfere. The model may adjust representations that were useful for language to make image generation better, especially if the diffusion loss dominates training. You can end up with better visual synthesis but weaker language semantics.

So it’s not that jointly learning text and images is inherently harmful. The concern is how you share the representations and balance the objectives. You want visual learning to enrich the model’s understanding without overwriting the structure it already learned from language.
